title: I Rebuilt My Home Network From Scratch
creator: Kai Nakamura
description:
I tore out my whole home network and rebuilt it: a fanless firewall, VLANs for the smart home junk, and PoE access points on every floor.

Sponsored by Vaultra. Get 3 months free plus 20% off your first year with code KAI: https://vaultra.com/kai

Parts list and firewall rules: in the pinned comment.

sentences.t: Six months ago my home network was a disaster.

I had a router from my internet provider, a mesh system I bought on sale, two switches I don't remember buying, and a smart plug that I'm pretty sure was talking to a server in a country I've never been to.
So I tore it all out, every cable, every box, and started over.
This video is the whole rebuild, what I bought, what I configured, and what I'd do differently.
Let's start with the plan.
I wanted three things.
First, fast and stable wifi in every room, including the garage, which has historically been a dead zone.
Second, all the smart home junk on its own network, completely separated from my computers.
And third, I wanted to actually understand what was going on, instead of just trusting a box with blinking lights.
For the core, I went with a small fanless mini PC running open source firewall software.
It's got four network ports, it sips about ten watts, and it replaced the provider's router entirely.
The provider's box is now in bridge mode, which basically means it passes the internet through and does nothing else.
Behind the firewall there's one managed switch, and this is where the magic happens, because it supports VLANs.
If you've never heard of VLANs, think of them as separate networks that share the same physical cables.
My computers and phones live on one, the smart home devices live on another, guests get a third, and the cameras get their own little jail with no internet at all.
That last one was a big deal for me.
Cheap cameras are notorious for phoning home, and now they physically can't, they can only talk to my recorder.
For wifi I used three ceiling-mounted access points, one per floor, all powered over the network cable, so there are no power bricks anywhere.
Running cable to the ceiling was easily the worst part of this project.
I spent one entire Saturday in the attic, in July, with a fish tape and a headlamp, and I do not recommend it.
But the result is full speed in the garage, which means I can finally watch tutorials while I'm pretending to fix my bike.
Once the hardware was in, I had to set up a ridiculous number of logins.
Firewall admin, switch admin, the controller for the access points, the camera recorder, a DNS filter, and about a dozen smart home accounts.
And honestly, that's the perfect moment to talk about today's sponsor, Vaultra, because juggling a pile of logins is exactly the problem it solves.
Vaultra is a password manager, and before you click away, hear me out, because I resisted using one for years.
My excuse was always that putting all of my passwords in one place sounded like a terrible idea.
What changed my mind was actually understanding how Vaultra stores your data.
Everything in your vault is encrypted on your own device before it ever leaves it, using a master password that Vaultra never sees and never stores.
So even if somebody broke into their servers, all they'd get is a pile of scrambled data they can't read.
They've also had the whole system audited by outside security firms, and they publish those reports, which is the kind of transparency I want from a company holding my keys.
Day to day, it's just easy.
When I sign up for something new, Vaultra offers to generate a long random password, saves it, and fills it in next time without me having to think about it.
It works in every browser I use, on my phone, on my laptop, and on my partner's tablet, and it all stays in sync.
There's a built-in authenticator too, so the six-digit two-factor codes live right next to the password instead of in a separate app I always forget to back up.
And the security dashboard is genuinely a bit scary, in a good way.
The first time I ran it, it told me I had forty-one reused passwords and three that had shown up in known data breaches.
One of them was an old forum login I'd completely forgotten about, and it was the same password I'd been using for my email.
I changed all of them in one evening, and Vaultra walked me through each one with a direct link to the right settings page.
The feature I didn't expect to love is secure sharing.
My family has a shared folder now with the streaming logins, the guest wifi password, and the account for our internet provider.
When my brother needs the login for my mom's streaming account, I don't text it to him in plain text anymore, I just share the item, and I can take it back any time.
There's also an emergency access feature, where you pick a trusted person who can request access to your vault if something happens to you.
That's not a fun thing to think about, but after helping my dad sort out my grandfather's accounts last year, I can tell you it matters a lot.
Vaultra has a free plan that covers unlimited passwords on one type of device, which is a fine way to try it out.
But the plan I'd point most people to is the family plan, which covers up to six people, each with their own private vault plus shared folders.
It costs less per month than a single streaming subscription, and it protects literally every other account you have.
If you've been meaning to sort out your passwords for years, like I was, this is your sign.

That's vaultra.com slash kai, code KAI, and the link is right at the top of the description.
Seriously, do it tonight, it takes about twenty minutes to move your important accounts over.
Thanks to Vaultra for supporting the channel.
Okay, back to the network.
With everything set up, I wanted to see if the separation actually worked, so I ran a few tests.
From my laptop, I tried to reach the smart plug directly, and the firewall blocked it, exactly like it should.
From the guest network, I tried to see my file server, and it couldn't even find it.
And the cameras, which I watched with a traffic monitor for a full week, made zero connections to the internet that got through.
They tried, by the way.
One of them tried to contact the same address about every ninety seconds, all day, which is both hilarious and deeply unsettling.
Speeds are great.
I'm getting the full gigabit on wired connections and around six hundred megabits on wifi in most of the house, including the garage.
So, what would I do differently?
First, I'd buy one access point with better range instead of fighting with placement for the upstairs one, which I moved three times.
Second, I'd label every cable at both ends on day one, because I didn't, and I regretted it within a week.
And third, I'd keep a written plan of which VLAN is which, because when something breaks at eleven at night, you do not want to be guessing.
Total cost was a bit over eight hundred dollars, which I know sounds like a lot, but it replaced a pile of stuff that was worse in every way.
If you want my full parts list and the firewall rules I used, they're in the pinned comment.
In the next video, I'm setting up a little server in the closet to run my own media library and backups, so stick around for that.
Thanks for watching, and I'll catch you next time.
